standard.title: Factors and multiples
standard.description: Express natural numbers as products of their factors, recognise multiples and determine if one number is divisible by another
standard.prior_knowledge: Students can identify odd and even numbers and recognise some basic number properties (AC9M4N02). They have not yet systematically expressed numbers as products of factors or applied divisibility reasoning.
standard.progression_endpoint: Students express natural numbers as products of their factors, recognise multiples, and determine divisibility.

nodes.label: Multiples
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can list multiples of a given number and recognise whether a number is a multiple of another.
nodes.minimum_width: List at least 10 multiples of any single-digit number; identify whether a given number is a multiple of a given factor.
nodes.typical_width: Generate multiples for numbers 2–12; use multiples to solve divisibility questions informally; identify common multiples.
wider: Use skip-counting patterns on a hundreds chart to visualise multiples
Connect multiples to real-world contexts (e.g. scheduling, tiling, packing)

response_modes.reason: Fluency with multiples is foundational for later fraction and LCM work. Students need repeated practice before the concept transfers reliably.

nodes.hinge_reason: Fluent multiple recognition is directly required by Node 2 (systematic factor pairs) and Node 4 (divisibility) — students who cannot reliably identify multiples cannot work systematically through factor pairs or apply divisibility rules.
success_criteria: Student lists multiples of a given number without skip-counting errors
Student determines whether a given number is a multiple of another and explains why

nodes.label: Factors and factor pairs
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can find all factor pairs of a natural number and list all its factors.
nodes.minimum_width: Find all factor pairs of a two-digit number using systematic division; list all factors in ascending order.
nodes.typical_width: Apply a systematic factor-pair strategy to numbers up to 100; distinguish between factors and multiples; identify numbers with only two factors (primes) as a pattern without naming them.
wider: Use rectangular arrays to model all factor pairs visually
Investigate why some numbers have an odd number of factors (perfect squares)

response_modes.reason: The systematic factor-pair approach (start from 1, work up to the square root) requires an explicit reasoning scaffold. Without it, students miss factors or double-count.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: Arrays and perfect square patterns give advancing students genuine mathematical structure to explore.
nodes.hinge_reason: Systematic factor-pair finding is the prerequisite for Node 3 (products of factors) — students who cannot reliably enumerate factor pairs cannot express numbers as products of multiple factors.
success_criteria: Student finds all factor pairs of a two-digit number systematically
Student lists all factors of a number in order without omissions

nodes.label: Products of factors
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can express a natural number as a product of two or more factors in multiple ways.
nodes.minimum_width: Express a given number as a product of two factors in at least two different ways (e.g. 24 = 4 × 6 = 3 × 8).
nodes.typical_width: Express numbers as products of more than two factors; connect to area models and array representations; recognise that multiplication is commutative across factor pairs.
wider: Explore factor trees as a visual representation of repeated factoring
Investigate which numbers can be expressed as products of two equal factors (perfect squares)
success_criteria: Student expresses a given number as a product of factors in multiple ways
Student verifies each product using multiplication

nodes.label: Divisibility
nodes.progression_checkpoint: Students can determine whether one natural number is divisible by another and explain their reasoning.
nodes.minimum_width: Determine whether a given number is divisible by 2, 5 or 10, explaining the rule used.
nodes.typical_width: Apply and explain divisibility patterns for 2, 3, 4, 5, 6, 9 and 10; connect divisibility to the factor relationship.
wider: Investigate divisibility patterns using digital tools to test large numbers
Explore how divisibility connects to factors and multiples in number grids (e.g. Sieve of Eratosthenes)

response_modes.reason: Students often over-generalise divisibility rules (e.g. applying the digit-sum rule to 4). Multiple number examples across different divisors help distinguish which rules apply where.

nodes.width_opportunity_reason: The Sieve and large-number digital investigation give advancing students rich pattern exploration territory.
success_criteria: Student correctly applies divisibility rules for at least three different divisors
Student connects divisibility to the factor relationship (if a÷b has no remainder, b is a factor of a)
